title: Radiative forcing of climate from halocarbon-induced global stratospheric ozone loss
problem: Existing assessments of greenhouse gas forcing from halocarbons have largely neglected the indirect cooling effect caused by the stratospheric ozone depletion these chemicals induce, thus potentially overestimating their net contribution to climate change.
method: We determine the radiative forcing of the surface-troposphere system from observed decadal ozone losses using two zonally averaged Fixed Dynamical Heating models, and compare it with the forcing from increased concentrations of other greenhouse gases over the same time period.
task: The task is to determine the radiative forcing on the climate system from observed stratospheric ozone loss and compare it to the forcing from other greenhouse gases, thereby re-evaluating the net climate impact of halocarbons.

innovation: This paper demonstrates that the radiative cooling caused by halocarbon-induced stratospheric ozone loss significantly offsets the direct greenhouse warming from these same gases, revealing that the net climate forcing from chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) is substantially less than previously estimated.

Net radiative (solar plus longwave) forcing due to the 1979-90 increases in CFCs and in all non-ozone gases, and that due to the observed stratospheric ozone losses. The net radiative forcing is obtained with the stratosphere in equilibrium in the presence of a fixed dynamical heating. The GFDL model results are averages over the four mid-season months, whereas the Reading model results (in parentheses) are averages over January and July only. Positive values denote gain of radiative energy.
